conclusion: A normal executable linked to the repository-local OpenCL/runtime stack is the product-level OpenCL gate. The fsynced daemon trace is authoritative for GPUDispatcher/ComputeUnit execution and lifecycle, while the application-side readback and oracle are authoritative for bytes delivered to the user.
decision: Require the ordinary host executable to compile the .cl source, manage gem5 without a manually started endpoint, submit and wait through the local runtime, read C back, validate the exact oracle, clean up the owner, and report zero CPU/NVIDIA fallback. Keep the CP26 generic endpoint as regression evidence only, and never infer delivered output from daemon CRC alone.
invalidated_assumptions: A manually launched protocol endpoint is equivalent to a normal OpenCL application.
A durable type-20 response by itself proves GPUDispatcher or ComputeUnit execution.
A daemon output CRC proves that the application received correct bytes without D2H verification.
Source compilation may silently use a system OpenCL, ROCr, HIP, CUDA, or hardware fallback path.
observation: Under a scrubbed environment, the normal opencl-vecadd executable links the local libOpenCL.so.1, compiles vecadd.cl with the pinned local compiler/device libraries, creates a private job and socket, supervises gem5, submits one dispatch, reads only C back, validates bit-exact C=A+B, unmaps, joins the daemon, and exits successfully. The daemon records the exact three-event execution trace; the client independently validates the returned C bytes.
question_or_symptom: What constitutes product-level OpenCL execution, and which side is authoritative for simulated execution versus bytes returned to the application?
